## There is a saying in Japanese, “When trees sink and rocks float.” It

## refers to occurrences that contravene the norm; but in the world of the novel—or perhaps, more broadly, in the realm of art—such reversals take place all the time. Things the world sees as trivial can acquire weight over time, while other things broadly considered to be weighty can, quite suddenly, reveal themselves to be only hollow shells.

The essay “When I Became a Novelist” introduces 30-year-old Murakami in a firecracker of a literary debut, winning the Gunzo Prize for New Writers with a short piece of juvenilia, Hear the Wind Sing (1979). With a tinge of impostor syndrome, he tells us that he thought it was an inadequate novella. It became the first installment of a trilogy, followed by Pinball, 1973 (1980) and the considerably more accomplished A Wild Sheep Chase (1982). novelist, to become part of the “literary industry.” Novelist as a Vocation is an indispensable contribution to understanding Murakami’s astounding mind and method.
